teaching_examples.target: Subject, finite verb and object in an ordinary main clause.
Fronted accusative object; case and agreement retain participant roles.

teaching_examples.text: Ðā hīerde se munuc ðone sang.
teaching_examples.translation: Then the monk heard the song.
teaching_examples.target: Initial adverb and a following finite verb before a nominal subject.

teaching_examples.text: Ðā hē ðone sang hīerde, ðā ēode hē tō ðǣm bisceope.
teaching_examples.translation: When he heard the song, he went to the bishop.
teaching_examples.target: Temporal conjunction and correlative adverb; dependent versus main-clause placement.

teaching_examples.text: Se sang wæs swēte. Hē wæs ēac wynsum.
teaching_examples.translation: The song was sweet. It was also pleasant.
teaching_examples.target: Masculine personal reference to a grammatically masculine inanimate antecedent.

teaching_examples.text: Se bisceop geseah ðone munuc and grētte hine.
teaching_examples.translation: The bishop saw the monk and greeted him.
teaching_examples.target: Continued subject through coordination; personal accusative retains the object.

teaching_examples.text: Se bisceop geseah ðone munuc. Hē wæs on ðǣm hūse.
teaching_examples.translation: The bishop saw the monk. He was in the house.
teaching_examples.target: The second sentence can refer to either man in a suitable context; morphology alone does not select one.

teaching_examples.text: Se bisceop cwæð: “Ic wille mid ēow sprecan.”
teaching_examples.translation: The bishop said, “I want to speak with you.”
teaching_examples.target: The bishop addresses several monks. Quoted person is interpreted from the speaker and addressees.

teaching_examples.text: Se munuc, ðe se bisceop grētte, ēode tō ðǣre cirican.
teaching_examples.translation: The monk whom the bishop greeted went to the church.
teaching_examples.target: A nominative antecedent is the object within its relative clause.

teaching_examples.text: Ðā se bisceop cōm, ðā sungon ðā brōðor.
teaching_examples.translation: When the bishop came, the brothers sang.
teaching_examples.target: Three identical surfaces serve as temporal conjunction, correlative adverb and article.

teaching_examples.text: Se bisceop wæs on ðǣm hūse, and se munuc on ðǣre cirican.
teaching_examples.translation: The bishop was in the house, and the monk in the church.
teaching_examples.target: Recover the repeated copula in the coordinated clause with a different expressed subject.

teaching_examples.text: Hē sægde ðæt se sang swēte wǣre.
teaching_examples.translation: He said that the song was sweet.
teaching_examples.target: Content-clause boundary and late finite subjunctive, with relative reporting time.

new_reading.title: The bishop and the monk
new_reading.text: Se bisceop sæt on ðǣm hūse, and se munuc wæs ðǣr. Ðā se munuc ðone sang hīerde, ðā ēode hē tō ðǣm bisceope. Se munuc cwæð: “Ic hīerde ðone sang, ðe swīðe wynsum wæs. Hīerdest ðū hine?” Se bisceop cwæð: “Gā nū, and lǣd ðā brōðor hider.” Ðā ēode se munuc tō ðǣre cirican, and cōm ęft mid ðǣm brōðrum. Se bisceop geseah hīe and cwæð: “Gē sindon mīne frīend. Ic wille mid ēow sprecan.” Se munuc sæt mid ðǣm brōðrum, and hīe hīerdon ðæs bisceopes word.
new_reading.rationale: A complete hearing, inquiry, summons and gathering. Explicit nouns, masculine reference to song, relative-clause embedding, temporal correlation, omitted repeated subject and quoted speaker/addressees prepare the checked Chad passage. This is an original account, not an adaptation or purported historical event.
